summary: Jesus declares that He came to fulfill the Law, then shows its true depth: anger, lust, broken promises and revenge judged at the heart, and love even for enemies.
key_insight: None of the six examples loosens the Law; each one asks for more. Jesus moves from murder to anger, from adultery to lust, from oaths to plain truth, and from limited revenge to love for enemies. That is the righteousness that exceeds the scribes and Pharisees.
story: “Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to destroy but to fulfill.” Not one jot or tittle would pass from the Law till all was fulfilled. Then Jesus startled His hearers: “unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven.” {Mt}

He gave six examples, setting what they had heard beside His own “But I say to you.” They had heard, “You shall not murder,” but He said that anger and contempt toward a brother already stand under judgment. Better to leave a gift at the altar and first be reconciled. They had heard, “You shall not commit adultery,” but whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery in his heart. Better to lose an eye or a hand than to have the whole body cast into hell. {Mt}

On divorce, He said that a man who divorces his wife for any reason except sexual immorality causes her to commit adultery. On oaths, “do not swear at all,” but “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’” {Mt}

They had heard, “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” But Jesus said, “I tell you not to resist an evil person.” {Mt} Turn the other cheek; let the man who sues for your tunic have your cloak as well; {Mt} if someone compels you to go one mile, go two; {Mt} give to the one who asks.

Last, they had heard, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” Jesus said, “love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you.” Then they would be sons of their Father, who makes His sun rise on the evil and the good. {Mt} Luke records the same call and adds, “And just as you want men to do to you, you also do to them likewise.” Lend, He said, “hoping for nothing in return.” {Lk}

Loving those who love you is nothing special. Even tax collectors do that, {Mt} and even sinners. {Lk} “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” {Mt} In Luke the call ends, “Therefore be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew gives the whole section on the Law, with six contrasts; Luke records only the teaching on loving enemies.
Luke places the Golden Rule here (6:31); Matthew places it later in the sermon (7:12).
Matthew ends, “be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect”; Luke ends, “be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.”
Matthew speaks of someone suing for your tunic; Luke of someone taking your cloak. The order of the two garments is reversed.
Matthew compares with tax collectors; Luke compares with sinners and adds the example of lending.

scene.label: Jot and tittle
scene.text: The jot is the yod, the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet. A tittle is a tiny stroke that tells one letter from another. Jesus means the smallest detail of Scripture.

scene.label: Raca, the council and hell
scene.text: Raca was an Aramaic insult, roughly empty-headed. The council was the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court. “Hell fire” translates a phrase built on Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31) and a picture of God’s final judgment.

scene.label: An eye for an eye
scene.text: This law (Exodus 21:24) was given to judges, to keep punishment in proportion to the crime. It was never meant as a license for private revenge, which is how Jesus’ hearers were tempted to use it.

scene.label: The second mile
scene.text: Roman soldiers could force a civilian to carry their gear for a mile, about a thousand paces, as soldiers later forced Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus’ cross (Matthew 27:32).

scene.label: “Hate your enemy”
scene.text: The Law said, “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). It never commanded hatred of enemies; that was a conclusion people drew by narrowing the word “neighbor.” Jesus removes the limit.

witnesses.matthew: Writing for readers steeped in the Law, Matthew gives Jesus’ full teaching on it: He came to fulfill, not destroy, and His “But I say to you” reaches to the heart. Matthew shows Jesus as the one who states God’s will with final authority, greater than Moses yet never against him.
witnesses.luke: Leaves out the debates over the Law and keeps the call to love enemies. Luke adds the Golden Rule and lending with no hope of return, and he ends not with perfection but with mercy: “be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.”

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as Lord of the Law, not one more interpreter of it. He fulfills it, states its true depth on His own word, and shows the Father as the One who sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust.
seeing.living: Jesus does not lower the standard; He shows what children of the Father look like. Bring Him the anger you excuse and the looks you justify, and pray by name for someone who has wronged you.
seeing.ponder: Who is the person you find hardest to love, and what would it mean to pray for them as your Father’s child?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus fulfills the Law by calling for a righteousness that begins in the heart.
preaching.watch_for: Verse 20 is the thesis and verse 48 the summary. In between, six times Jesus sets what was said beside His own word: five times “But I say to you” (vv. 22, 28, 32, 34, 44) and once “But I tell you” (v. 39).

title: Jesus and the Law
